list.listitem: Urinary catheterization should be discouraged as a means of obtaining urine for culture or other diagnostic tests when the patient can voluntarily void or as a substitute for nursing care in the incontinent patient.
Indications for short-term catheterization: acute urinary retention, urinary tract and other surgery, and accurate monitoring of urinary output in acutely ill patients.

Indications for long-term catheterization: (1) Chronic urinary retention or neurogenic bladder in patients unable to perform intermittent self-catheterization; (2) urinary incontinence associated with intractable skin breakdown; (3) comfort care for terminally ill or severely impaired incontinent patients.

list.listitem: Recent reconstructive surgery of urethra or bladder.
Known or suspected urethral disruption secondary to trauma.
Known or suspected urethral stricture.
Counsel patient about the indications, risks, benefits, and alternatives (condom catheters, intermittent self-catheterization, suprapubic catheterization).

A recent Cochrane review concluded that in general, evidence was insufficient to determine if one route of bladder drainage (indwelling vs intermittent catheterisation vs suprapubic catheterisation) is more likely to reduce urinary tract infections than another. It also concluded that suprapubic catheters are associated with less pain compared to indwelling catheters.
Position the patient appropriately (lithotomy position for female patients, supine position for males).
Cleanse the urethral meatus and surrounding area with antiseptic solution and use sterile drapes to isolate the genital area.
Maintain sterile technique throughout the procedure.
Lubricate the urethra with sterile surgical lubricant or 2% lidocaine jelly using a 10 mL syringe.

Select appropriate catheter: 16 or 18 French catheter for adults. Foley (straight tip) catheter for females. Foley (straight tip) or coude (curved tip) catheter for males younger than 50 years. Coudé catheter for males older than 50 years.

Pass the catheter through the urethra into the bladder using a smooth and continuous motion being careful never to use excessive force. When using a Coudé catheter, the curved tip of the catheter should be at the 12 o'clock position during insertion to facilitate passage through the bladder neck, which may be elevated due to benign prostatic hypertrophy. For females, pass the catheter until urine return from the bladder is noted. For males, pass the full length of the catheter to the balloon inflation port into the urethra to prevent inflation of the balloon in the proximal urethra.
Inflate balloon with 5 mL of sterile water after correct placement of catheter in bladder is confirmed by appropriate urine return.

Secure the catheter in a neutral position and without tension. For females the catheter should be secured with tape or other device to the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. For males the catheter should be secured with tape or other device to the anterior abdominal wall.
Routinely inspect the catheter and urethral meatus to ensure that the catheter is properly secured and that there is no injury to the meatus.
In the disoriented or combative patient, restraints may be necessary to prevent significant urethral trauma.
Continually reassess the need for catheterization and remove catheter as soon as clinically prudent.
A Cochrane review found 68 studies with 9247 participants comparing shorter with longer duration of catheterization
See for recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention regarding catheter management.

A meta-analysis of six studies with 1520 patients found that 1 to 3 doses of an antibiotic (ciprofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, and cefotaxime were studied) cut the likelihood of infection in the next 6 weeks from 10.5% to 4.7%.

Among women undergoing surgery for stress incontinence and prolapse, home catheter removal was noninferior to office removal for early retention (11.9% vs. 22.4%, P = .13) and resulted in fewer office visits. Home removal was associated with less pain (P = .02) and higher likelihood of reuse (P = .004), with no differences in difficulty or satisfaction.
Bacteruria is inevitable with prolonged catheterization.
Prevention of infection should be the main goal.

Urinary tract infections are the most common nosocomial infection accounting for nearly 40% of hospital-acquired infections, and about 80% of these UTIs are associated with urinary catheters. Catheter-associated urinary tract infections may confer a nearly 3-fold increase in mortality among hospitalized patients.
Continuously closed system of urinary drainage is the cornerstone of infection control.

A meta-analysis of 6 studies with 1520 patients found that 1 to 3 doses of an antibiotic (ciprofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, and cefotaxime were studied) cut the likelihood of infection in the next 6 weeks from 10.5% to 4.7%.
Antibiotic treatment is indicated only in patients with symptomatic infections and antibiotic therapy should be culture-directed.

Replacing chronic indwelling catheters before instituting antimicrobial therapy in elderly nursing home residents with an acute urinary tract infection hastens recovery, reduces reinfection rates, and may decrease mortality.

A recent Cochrane Review concluded that silver alloy and antibiotic coated urinary catheters may be helpful in reducing the risk of catheter-associated UTIs, although the cost effectiveness and the risks of microbial resistance with their use have yet to be clearly defined.

404 adults who performed clean intermittent self-catheterisation, and who had suffered at least 2 urinary tract infections in the previous year or had been hospitalized for urinary tract infection, were randomized to oral antibiotic prophylaxis (50 mg of nitrofurantoin, 100 mg of trimethoprim or 250 mg of cefalexin) or no prophylaxis for 12 months. Symptomatic UTI was decreased by 48% using prophylaxis however as expected the development of antimicrobial resistance was seen more frequently in those treated with antibiotic prophylaxis.

Long-term Foley catheterization significantly increases the risk of urinary complications (strictures, stones, fistulas, and obstruction), with the highest risk observed in men for urinary tract cancer (HR 6.6, 95% CI: 5.8-7.4) and other complications, while women had the highest risk for urinary tract infections.

Significant urethral injury, including creation of a false passage, can be inflicted due to traumatic attempts at insertion of a urinary catheter. Injury occurs most commonly in patients with preexisting urethral stricture or prostatic enlargement.
Balloon inflation in the urethra during catheter placement and inadvertent withdrawal of the catheter with the balloon inflated are other potential causes of urethral injury.
Most urethral injuries can be prevented with the use of proper insertion techniques and by avoiding excessive force during insertion.
Erosion of the glans penis can occur as a result of long-term catheterization and can be prevented by properly securing the catheter with no tension following the anatomic course of the urethra.
Urethral stricture is a common sequelae of long-term catheterization and should be suspected in patients with obstructive voiding symptoms and history of catheterization.
If significant catheter-related urethral injury is suspected, a urologist should be consulted for further evaluation and management.

Catheterization causes irritation of the bladder wall resulting in a wide variety of histologic changes ranging from nonneoplastic inflammatory changes to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder in patients requiring long-term indwelling catheters.
The need for catheterization should be continually reassessed and catheters should be removed as soon as clinically prudent.
Patients with spinal cord injury and indwelling catheters are at increased risk of developing bladder cancer compared with the general population (RR = 4.9; 95% CI, 1.2-13.8).
Patients requiring long-term indwelling catheters should be referred to a urologist annually, at a minimum, for surveillance evaluation.
Leakage of urine from the urethra around the catheter is not uncommon and is usually associated with bladder spasm.
Antispasmodic agents such as oxybutynin or hyoscyamine can be effective in alleviating bladder spasm.
Obstruction of the catheter with resultant urinary retention can also result in leakage and must be ruled out.
Blood clots can result in catheter obstruction in patients with gross hematuria.

The bladder should be irrigated using 1 liter of normal saline instilled into the catheter using a 60 mL syringe to evacuate the clot and determine if there is ongoing bleeding. If the irrigant clears, no further immediate treatment is necessary. If the irrigant does not clear, a urologist should be consulted for further evaluation and management as the patient may require continuous bladder irrigation via a triple-lumen catheter and cystoscopy.

Catheters are prone to develop encrustations due to the relative saturation of urine with substances such as calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, struvite, and other organic material which can eventually result in obstruction. The rate of encrustation and subsequent obstruction varies reflecting metabolic differences among patients.
Obstructed catheters should be removed and replaced if continued catheterization is clinically indicated.
Occasionally, a catheter cannot be removed when the balloon fails to deflate secondary to malfunction of the inflation valve or obstruction of the inflation channel by debris or crystals.
The inflation port can be cut distal to the junction with the catheter which may allow the balloon to deflate.
Injection of air or water into the inflation port in an attempt to rupture the balloon should be avoided as this may result in retained balloon fragments in the bladder.
If initial maneuvers are unsuccessful, a urologist should be consulted for further evaluation and management.

Noninfectious complications such as pain, urinary urgency, and hematuria are 5 times more likely to be reported than infectious complications among patients with an indwelling urethral catheter placed in the hospital for 3 to 30 days.

feature.caption: Summary of Major Recommendations from the CDC Guidelines for Prevention & Control of Catheter-associated UTIs.
feature.feature_body:
Category I. Strongly Recommended for Adoption
Educate personnel in correct techniques of catheter insertion and care.
Catheterize only when necessary.
Emphasize hand washing.
Insert catheter using aseptic technique and sterile equipment.
Secure catheter properly.
Maintain closed sterile drainage.
Obtain urine samples aseptically.
Maintain unobstructed urine flow.
Category II. Moderately Recommended for Adoption
Periodically re-educate personnel in catheter care.
Use smallest suitable bore catheter.
Avoid irrigation unless needed to prevent or relieve obstruction.
Refrain from daily meatal care.
Do not change catheters at arbitrary fixed intervals.
Category III. Weakly Recommended for Adoption
Consider alternative techniques of urinary drainage before using an indwelling urethral catheter.
Replace the collecting system when sterile closed drainage has been violated.
Spatially separate infected and uninfected patients with indwelling catheters.
Avoid routine bacteriologic monitoring.
Data from Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-associated Urinary Tract Infections (CDC, 2009-11-21).
